title: The Client That Hated My Work
author: Andrea Chiarelli
summary: Andrea Chiarelli uses a professional services scenario -- a new director who inherited a project he hadn't commissioned and immediately rejected it -- to illustrate the leadership concept of being a 'heat shield.' When a key stakeholder changed mid-project and declared the work too strategic, Chiarelli's instinct to defend the work rationally would have been satisfying and counterproductive. Instead of defending, he absorbed the friction, shielded his junior colleague from the pressure, and reframed his approach to the client: not 'here's why we did it' but 'help me understand what success looks like for you.' Within two weeks, the new director was citing the same work approvingly. Leadership in ambiguous, high-friction moments is not about defending quality but about managing the human dynamics that determine whether good work can land.
points: The heat shield metaphor from space flight captures a specific leadership function: during re-entry (when friction is most extreme), something must absorb the heat so the rest of the mission can survive intact.

Defending good work rationally to a skeptical new stakeholder is satisfying and counterproductive because the issue is rarely work quality -- it is whether the stakeholder has had the opportunity to shape and claim ownership.
Shielding junior team members from client friction is a specific skill: a colleague who has built something and suddenly had validation withdrawn needs enough stability to keep thinking clearly.

Asking 'help me understand what success looks like for you' instead of 'here's why we did what we did' gives skeptical clients room to reshape engagement on their terms -- which is often what they need to claim ownership.

When ambiguity spikes and uncertainty becomes contagious, someone must hold the pressure without transferring it; this is not emotional suppression but preserving the team's capacity to think and act.
quotes: Most leadership advice focuses on what to say: the right framework, the right question or the right way to present a decision. That's useful up to a point. But the moments that actually test whether you can lead tend to arrive without warning, and they don't care how good your framework is.

In space flight, re-entry is the dangerous part, because friction becomes extreme. The atmosphere doesn't care that your design is elegant. You always need a heat shield to absorb the heat long enough for everything else to survive the descent.

The team felt it immediately. A more junior colleague had built the core of the deliverable and had been getting positive feedback for weeks. Overnight, that validation disappeared. You could see the energy shift in our conversation, and my colleague started second-guessing their own work and hedging their language.

My immediate instinct was to get the new lead on a call and walk them through the rationale behind every decision. Essentially, defend the work and show them the evidence trail. That would have been satisfying and completely counterproductive, because the issue was never the quality of the work.
